subtitulo: Attacking the assumption, not the person
descripcion: English separates the strength of a disagreement from its social temperature more sharply than Spanish does. You can reject an idea completely and still sound collaborative, and the mechanism is almost entirely formulaic — which means it is learnable in a week. The core move: attack the idea, never the person, and always leave the other position somewhere to stand.

filas: Help me understand how that would work in practice.
you suspect it collapses and want them to find it
I see it differently, and here's why.
I'd challenge the assumption underneath that.
the logic is fine, the starting point isn't
I hear you, but I don't think that follows.
I'm going to push back on that.
direct but still not hostile; very standard
reserve for when you mean it

ejemplos.texto: *I'd challenge the assumption underneath that rather than the conclusion — you're assuming the failure mode is technical.*
*Help me understand how that would work with a 200-millisecond budget.*
*I hear you, but I don't think the second half follows from the first.*
*I'm going to push back on that.*
*That's true of small systems, less so of anything safety-critical.*

notas: *I'm afraid I disagree* is textbook English and sounds slightly antique in speech. Fine in writing.
Attacking the *assumption* rather than the *conclusion* is the highest-value C1 move: it lets the other person retreat without losing face.
*With respect* is a warning sign in British English — it almost always precedes a demolition. Use knowingly or not at all.

contraste.es: Spanish softens disagreement with formulas like no sé si estoy del todo de acuerdo, which corresponds well to I'm not sure I entirely agree. A literal no estoy de acuerdo (I don't agree) sounds blunter in English professional contexts than it usually does in Spanish.
contraste.de: Das sehe ich etwas anders corresponds exactly to I see it slightly differently, a very useful diplomatic formula. The literal I am of another opinion sounds stiff; I'm not sure I agree is the natural English choice.
contraste.it: Non sono del tutto d'accordo corresponds well to I don't entirely agree, and la vedo un po' diversamente to I see it slightly differently. Diplomatic disagreement therefore transfers directly.
contraste.fr: Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord corresponds well to I don't entirely agree, and je vois les choses un peu différemment to I see it slightly differently. Diplomatic disagreement therefore transfers directly.
contraste.pt: Não concordo inteiramente corresponds well to I don't entirely agree, and vejo isso de outra forma to I see it differently. Diplomatic disagreement therefore transfers directly.

errores: *You are wrong* — grammatically fine, socially expensive, rare in professional English.
Softening until the disagreement disappears. If nobody noticed you disagreed, you didn't.
*No, but…* as an opener. Reverse it: *Yes, and here's the difficulty…*

es: *I am not agree* — a fossilised Spanish-speaker error worth naming once and killing.
de: Carrying over German directness: *That's not correct* or *I disagree* with no cushioning, which is neutral in German meetings but sounds combative in English.
it: *Guarda, …* as an opener rendered as *Look, …*, which sounds confrontational in English, instead of *I see it a bit differently*.
fr: *Écoute, …* as an opener rendered as *Listen, …*, which sounds confrontational in English, instead of *I see it a bit differently*.
pt: *Olha, …* as an opener rendered as *Look, …*, which sounds confrontational in English, instead of *I see it a bit differently*.

mision.consigna: Disagree with a confident claim about AI made by someone senior to you.
requisitos: use four different formulas from the reference box
never open a sentence with *but* or *no*

microtareas.texto: Take a claim you disagree with and write the assumption underneath it in one sentence.
Rewrite three blunt disagreements as questions.
Record 90 seconds disagreeing with: *AI will make junior engineers unnecessary.*

autochequeo: Did I attack an assumption, or only the conclusion?
Would a reader know I disagreed, or did I soften it away?
Any sentence that would read as rude to a British or American colleague?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on how I disagree. (1) Mark each disagreement formula and rate its social temperature from 1 to 5. (2) Tell me whether I attacked the assumption or only the conclusion. (3) Flag anywhere I softened so much the disagreement vanished. (4) Flag anything that would read as rude. Do not rewrite the text.
